content.text: Cross-validation doesn't build the model you deploy. It estimates how well your whole recipe, preprocessing, model and settings, performs on data it hasn't seen. The fold models are scaffolding: keeping the best one keeps the luckiest split, and its perfect fold score turned into 0.958 on a test set. Report the mean and spread of all folds, then refit the recipe on all your training data.
A developer trains a tumor classifier on scikit-learn's breast cancer dataset and runs 5-fold cross-validation with
return_estimator=True

. One fold scores a perfect 1.000. They pickle that fold's model, and the model card reads "accuracy: 100% (cross-validated)". On the held-out test set the model scores 0.958, exactly what a plain model trained on all the data gets. The "winning" fold model was never special.
The common misconception
Many developers see cross-validation as a way to produce the final model: run k folds, keep the model from the best one, and report its score. It's easy to see why:

items.text: hands you k fitted models, and they look like candidates.
Keeping the highest scorer looks like model selection, which is what cross-validation is famous for.
The best fold's score is real: it was measured on rows that model never trained on.

content.text: The half-truth: every fold score is a genuine held-out score. But each one measures a single split of the data, and the k models are trained the same way on almost the same rows. Picking among them picks among splits, not models.
What actually happens
Cross-validation
answers one question: if I train this recipe on data like mine, how well will the result do on rows it hasn't seen? It answers by building temporary models and throwing them away.
It evaluates a recipe, not a model

The scikit-learn user guide describes the loop: a model is trained on k-1 folds, validated on the remaining one, and the performance reported by k-fold cross-validation is the average of the values computed in the loop. What's being scored is the procedure, the preprocessing, the algorithm and its
hyperparameters
, applied to a training set. That's why
cross_val_score
returns an array of scores and nothing else.
cross_validate
can keep the fold estimators if you ask for them, which is useful for inspecting coefficients across folds, not for shipping.
Fold scores differ because the folds differ

With 426 development rows and 5 folds, each fold model trains on about 341 rows that overlap heavily with every other fold's training rows. The models end up nearly alike. What changes is the test fold: about 85 different rows each time, where a single mistake moves accuracy by more than a point. The fold that scored 1.000 got the easiest 85 rows, not the best model.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate, train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_dev, X_te, y_dev, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25,
                                            stratify=y, random_state=0)
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression())
cv = cross_validate(model, X_dev, y_dev, cv=5, return_estimator=True)
best = cv["test_score"].argmax()
deployed = cv["estimator"][best]  # "the winning fold's model"
print(f"fold scores {cv['test_score'].round(3)}")
print(f"reported    {cv['test_score'][best]:.3f}")
print(f"test set    {deployed.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")
# fold scores [0.953 0.976 0.965 0.976 1.   ]
# reported    1.000
# test set    0.958

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_dev, X_te, y_dev, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25,
                                            stratify=y, random_state=0)
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression())
scores = cross_val_score(model, X_dev, y_dev, cv=5)  # judges the recipe
print(f"CV estimate {scores.mean():.3f} +/- {scores.std():.3f}")
final = model.fit(X_dev, y_dev)  # the model you ship: all 426 dev rows
print(f"test set    {final.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")
# CV estimate 0.974 +/- 0.015
# test set    0.958

content.text: The same recipe scores between 0.953 and 1.000 depending only on which rows land in the test fold. Keeping the maximum of five noisy scores reports the luckiest one, 1.000, for a model that scores 0.958 on new rows. The mean of all five, 0.974 with a standard deviation of 0.015, is the honest estimate, and the test score sits about one standard deviation below it, well within the noise the folds already showed.
Refit on everything, then ship

A fold model has also seen only 80% of your development data. Deploying it throws away a fifth of your labeled rows for no benefit. Once cross-validation has told you the recipe works, train it one more time on all the development data: that's the model you ship. Here it scores 0.958 on the test set, the same as the "winning" fold model, with no lucky split behind its reputation.
scikit-learn's search tools follow the same pattern.
GridSearchCV
uses cross-validation to compare settings, then, with
refit=True
, its default, refits an estimator with the best parameters on the whole dataset you passed to
fit
best_estimator_
is that refit model, not one of the fold models.
Report the spread, not just the mean

The standard deviation across folds tells you how much the estimate depends on the split. The scikit-learn guide's own example prints the mean accuracy together with its standard deviation. When two recipes differ by less than that spread, the gap may be noise; a later article in this path covers comparing models properly.

The best fold holds the best model
It held the easiest rows: the 1.000 fold's model scored 0.958 on the test set
Report the mean and spread of all folds: 0.974 ± 0.015
Cross-validation replaces the final training run
After cross-validation, refit the recipe on all the training data

blocks.title: Let the search refit for you

content.text: When you tune with
GridSearchCV
or
RandomizedSearchCV
, keep the default
refit=True
and ship
best_estimator_
. It's already trained on all the data you gave the search, with the winning settings.

blocks.title: A CV score you chose by is no longer neutral

content.text: Using cross-validation to pick between recipes is fine, but the winner's mean score is then the best of several noisy estimates, the same trap as the best fold. Keep a separate test set for the final number, as the scikit-learn guide recommends, and score it once.
cross_val_predict

returns a prediction for every row from the fold model that didn't train on it. The guide notes these come from several distinct models undistinguished, so they're not an appropriate measure of generalization error. Use them for plots and diagnostics, and
cross_val_score
for the number.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Put the whole recipe in a pipeline

content.text: Wrap preprocessing and the model in a
Pipeline
, so each fold fits the scaler and the model only on its own training part.
Run
cross_val_score
or
cross_validate
on the development data and report the mean with the standard deviation, not any single fold.
Use cross-validation results to compare settings, features or algorithms. Never pick among the fold models themselves.

items.title: Refit the winner on all development data

content.text: Call
fit
on the full development set, or let
GridSearchCV
refit it, and ship that model.

items.title: Confirm once on the test set

content.text: Score the refit model on the held-out test set one time, and report that number alongside the CV estimate.
Key takeaways

items.text: Cross-validation estimates how a recipe performs on unseen data; it doesn't build your final model.
Fold scores differ by the luck of the split: the 1.000 fold's model scored 0.958 on the test set.
Report the mean and spread across all folds, 0.974 ± 0.015 here, never the best fold.
Refit the chosen recipe on all your training data, then confirm it on the test set once.
